paras: The attempted lynching of Taylor Gibbs took place at Lancaster, Garrard County, Kentucky, on 25 November 1903, when crowds of local citizens sought to hang Gibbs, a Black man accused of attempting to assault two white women on the road to Kirksville. County Attorney James Hamilton persuaded the crowd at the jail to disperse by promising an immediate indictment and trial. Gibbs was indicted two days later and sentenced to seven years in the penitentiary, and the wire reports presented the episode as a lynching prevented by the prosecutor's plea.

Gibbs, described by the Lancaster Central Record as about nineteen and the son of "Black Suse," had driven a traveling salesman to Kirksville that day. On his way back he met a woman and her daughter driving home from Lancaster, whom the local papers named as Mrs. Jack Hendren and Miss Mollie Hendren. According to the Stanford Interior Journal he pulled the daughter from the buggy, while the Central Record said he grabbed at the bridle and then the buggy before the women whipped their horse past him.

A telephone message brought a posse out from Lancaster; the Frankfort wire said the women reported the attack to a farmer, Joe Burnside, who made the call. The posse found Gibbs near W. S. Ferguson's farm and took him to the Hendren home, where he was identified, though the Central Record said he protested his innocence throughout. On the way back the posse met "a band of infuriated citizens" who, the Central Record wrote, would have hanged him had officers not said they were uncertain he was the right man.

By the time the party reached town the Public Square was full, and cries of "Hang him!" rose as Gibbs was hurried into jail. Hamilton came out and told the crowd that the grand jury then in session would indict at once and that Gibbs would be sent promptly to the penitentiary, after which the crowd left. A Lancaster dispatch of 27 November reported the jail still closely guarded amid rumors that a mob was forming in the upper end of the county.

With no court on Thanksgiving, the grand jury returned an indictment on Friday, 27 November, and Gibbs was tried at once. The jury gave him seven years, which the Central Record called "the limit of the law under the circumstances," and the Interior Journal dated the sentence to Saturday. The sheriff was to take him to the prison at Frankfort the following Monday.

The Central Record added that another Black prisoner, "Ugs," held for breaking into the depot, would also have been hanged had the jail been entered; the Interior Journal's Lancaster column reported that Anderson Sutton received five years for that break-in.

Outside Kentucky the story ran as a Frankfort wire item crediting the county attorney, headlined in the New York Sun "Saved from Mob Violence" and carried twice by the St. Louis Republic. The wire placed the jail at "Stanford" or "Stamford," named the women as Hamilton rather than Hendren, and stated that Gibbs had confessed.

The local papers were openly hostile to Gibbs, calling him "the brute" and "the scoundrel," and the Interior Journal wrote that Garrard County people were "naturally greatly incensed." Under the headline "Almost A Lynching," the Central Record praised the crowd as "substantial citizens" and wrote that, while it did not advocate violence, leaving both prisoners "swinging in the Park" would have had "a decidedly good effect." Kentucky papers in Richmond, Berea and Jackson carried short state dispatches on the guarded jail and the speedy trial, and no Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The wire's report that Gibbs "confessed" conflicts with the Central Record's statement that he protested his innocence, and the Lancaster paper's fuller account, written by a paper in the town where he was held, gives the more detailed version. The local papers and the Lancaster dispatches place the jail and crowd at Lancaster, while the Frankfort wire puts them at Stanford.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Taylor Gibbs
bases: A crowd gathered to hang Taylor Gibbs, a Black prisoner accused of assault, first on the road and then at the jail, and dispersed on the county attorney's promise of a quick trial (A1, A4, A9).
Gibbs was not killed: the crowds that cried for his hanging dispersed and he was tried and sentenced to seven years (A3, A5, A9), so this was an attempted or threatened lynching, not a completed one.

Two local papers (A4, A9), a separate Frankfort wire (A1, A3) and Lancaster state dispatches (A6, A10) agree that a crowd sought to lynch Gibbs, that he was kept in jail, and that he was sentenced to seven years.

accounts.label: Frankfort wire
accounts.gist: Gibbs, arrested 'at Stanford' after trying to stop the Hamilton women's buggy, was captured and 'confessed'; a mob at the jail was talked down by County Attorney Hamilton's promise of a prompt trial.

accounts.label: Stanford Interior Journal
accounts.gist: Gibbs pulled Miss Mollie Hendren from the buggy; he was brought to Lancaster, where 'an attempt to lynch him proved futile'.

accounts.label: Lancaster Central Record
accounts.gist: Gibbs grabbed at the bridle and buggy but the women escaped; a posse identified him while he protested his innocence; a band on the road would have hanged him but officers said they were not sure he was the right man; Hamilton calmed the crowd on the Public Square.

accounts.label: Kentucky state dispatches from Lancaster
accounts.gist: The jail stayed under close guard on Nov. 27 amid rumors of a mob; Gibbs was indicted, tried and sentenced to seven years.

framing.detail: The national wire headlined the county attorney's success ('Saved from Mob Violence', 'Prevents a Lynching') and reported the accusation and a confession as fact.
The Stanford paper called Gibbs 'the brute' and 'the scoundrel' and said Garrard people were 'naturally greatly incensed', while recording the lynching attempt as 'futile'.
The Lancaster Central Record ('Almost A Lynching') praised the crowd as 'substantial citizens' and wrote that leaving Gibbs and 'Ugs' hanging in the park 'would have had a decidedly good effect'.

conflicts.note: Both local papers, including Stanford's own, put the jail and crowd at Lancaster, and the Lancaster-datelined dispatch speaks of the jail there; the Stanford placement comes only from the Frankfort wire.
